name: John Brown
role: American abolitionist; led the Pottawatomie killings (1856) and the Harpers Ferry raid (1859)
summary: Brown was an evangelical Christian who held that slavery was a war against the enslaved and that it should be ended by force. He led killings in Kansas and an armed raid on a federal armory, and drew up a provisional constitution for a free government of the oppressed. His surviving writings address slavery, religion and the organization of his provisional government, and say little about wider economic or foreign policy.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: Brown's Provisional Constitution opens by invoking the 'eternal and self-evident truths' of the Declaration of Independence against slavery, and in his 2 November 1859 speech he said God is no 'respecter of persons' and that acting for 'His despised poor' was right. Wikipedia reports he treated the Golden Rule and 'all men are created equal' as meaning the same thing.

political-violence-never.rationale: He led the Pottawatomie killings (1856) and the Harpers Ferry raid (1859), and his last note said the crimes of the land would never be purged away 'but with blood'. He held armed force to be justified against slavery.

initiating-force-wrong.rationale: He personally led armed attacks, including the seizure of the federal armory, to free slaves. His Constitution calls slavery a 'War' already waged on the enslaved, so he treated his force as a response, but he started the fighting at Harpers Ferry.

revolution-justified.rationale: He set up a provisional government and army to end slavery by force, but Article XLVI says the Constitution is not meant to overthrow any State or the general government and looks only to 'Amendment and Repeal'. The evidence points both ways.

armed-group-creates-revolution.rationale: Wikipedia reports he expected that once he began the first battle, slaves would rise across the South. At trial he denied any intent to incite insurrection, so the evidence is contested.

direct-action.rationale: Wikipedia records him dismissing pacifist abolitionists ('What we need is action'), and he founded the League of Gileadites and led raids and rescues instead of relying on petitions or politics. He also held a constitutional convention, so this is not an exclusive rejection of institutions.

state-arms-monopoly.rationale: He led a private armed force against state and federal authority, and his Constitution creates its own army and encourages members to carry arms openly. It also bars concealed weapons and has non-members found armed seized in territory it holds.

abolish-armed-forces.rationale: His Provisional Constitution creates a Commander-in-Chief, a Secretary of War and an army, and he commanded armed forces in Kansas and at Harpers Ferry.

people-in-arms.rationale: Article XLIII encourages all suitable members, male or female, to carry arms openly, but the same Constitution sets up a commissioned army with a Commander-in-Chief, so it is not a replacement of the army by citizens.

limit-guns.rationale: Article XLIII encourages members to carry arms openly, while Articles XLIV-XLV ban concealed weapons and have non-members found armed seized. The provisions point both ways.

defensive-wars-only.rationale: He started the armed seizure of the armory, though he described slavery as an existing war on the enslaved, so he framed his action as defensive. Contested.

more-religion-public.rationale: His Constitution provides for schools and churches, a Sabbath for religious instruction, and civil officers 'of first-rate moral and religious character'.

laws-from-scripture.rationale: In his speech he told the court the 'law of God' in the Bible taught the Golden Rule and obligations to those in bonds, and he said he acted on it. His Constitution also enforces Sabbath rest and bans profane swearing.

separate-church-state.rationale: The provisional constitution requires religious qualifications in recruitment and organizes public religious teaching and Sabbath observance.

religion-illusion.rationale: He was an evangelical Christian who said he acted as 'an instrument of God' and under the Bible's teaching.

women-suffrage.rationale: Article I covers all persons of mature age in the oppressed races together with the enslaved, Article III has all mature citizens of the organization elect the Congress, and Article XLIII refers to 'male or female' members. Eligibility for office is not stated.

premarital-sex.rationale: Article XL of his Constitution forbids 'unlawful intercourse of the sexes', and Article XLII requires respect for the marriage relation.

abolish-legal-marriage.rationale: Inferred: Article XLII requires that 'the marriage relation shall be at all times respected' and families kept together, which points against abolishing legal marriage. He did not address its legal benefits.

racial-franchise.rationale: His Constitution (adopted at Chatham by 34 Black and 12 white delegates, per Wikipedia) gives the vote to all mature members of the organization and protects white slaveholders who free their slaves, not one racial group alone.

racial-segregation-law.rationale: Inferred: he held all people equal before God and the Declaration, and his organization and its Constitution were open to Black and white members alike.

correct-racial-injustice.rationale: No recorded position found: the evidence found addresses a nearby question, not this statement.

slavery-not-civil-war-cause.rationale: Inferred: he died before the war, but his last note said the 'crimes of this guilty land' would be purged only with blood, tying coming bloodshed to slavery.

property-fundamental.rationale: Article XXXVI confiscates the property of people acting for the enemy or 'wilfully holding slaves', Article XXVIII holds the captured and common property of members for the whole equally, and he took slaves from owners in Missouri.

priority-to-poor.rationale: In his speech he said that acting for 'His despised poor' was right, and that had he acted for the rich and powerful he would have been rewarded. This concerns his cause, not a general welfare programme.

rehabilitation.rationale: Article XXII sets 'hard labor on the public works' as punishment for non-capital crimes, and Article XXXII requires kind treatment of prisoners. The first points towards punishment, the second does not conflict with it.

abolish-police-prisons.rationale: His Constitution provides a supreme court, courts-martial, a civil police 'always in readiness' and punishment by hard labor.

sovereign-above-law.rationale: His Constitution lets the President, Vice President, judges and Commander-in-Chief be tried and removed for misconduct, and bars removal of officers without a fair trial.

elective-rulers.rationale: His Constitution has the President, Vice President and judges chosen by the citizens or members, and Congress elected for three-year terms.

property-franchise.rationale: His Constitution lets all citizens of mature age and sound mind in the organization vote, with no property or tax qualification.

unjust-law-not-binding.rationale: He called slaveholding enactments 'wicked, cruel, and unjust' and founded the League of Gileadites to resist the Fugitive Slave Act. He appealed to the 'law of God' over the courts, but did not state the principle in general terms.

no-duty-to-obey.rationale: He knowingly broke slave and fugitive laws on grounds of conscience, but his Constitution demands 'implicit obedience to law' within his own organization, so his view is mixed.

self-ownership.rationale: Inferred: his opposition to slavery as a 'barbarous' war on the enslaved, and his aim of freeing them, follow from a claim that people own themselves. He did not state it in those terms.

bound-labor.rationale: Inferred: he devoted his life to ending compulsory bondage of labor, and the Constitution protects families and requires voluntary service only for the common good. He did not discuss serfdom.

reason-over-faith.rationale: His final family letter affirms the Bible’s divine source and eternal life, urging reason to examine and confirm scripture rather than replace it.

no-religion-state-schools.rationale: Article XLII of his provisional constitution calls for schools and churches giving religious as well as other instruction; it is an unenacted plan and does not clearly mean state schools.

separated-powers.rationale: Article II establishes separate legislative, executive and judicial branches; later articles distribute appointment, impeachment and removal powers among them.

head-commands-forces.rationale: Article VII of his draft constitution puts army movements under a distinct commander, not the president alone; an unenacted plan.

budget-needs-parliament.rationale: Congress appropriates public resources under Article XI, but Article XXX separately empowers the commander to draw on the intelligence fund with the war secretary’s countersignature.

consumerism-harmful.rationale: Sambo’s Mistakes, section III, criticizes expensive clothing, ornaments, fashionable entertainment and appetite indulgence that prevent useful work and helping others.

second-chamber.rationale: Articles II–III establish a single legislative house, rather than a bicameral legislature.

spiritual-nature.rationale: His political constitution provides moral and religious instruction, while his final family letter treats the soul and eternal life as realities.

racial-group-interests.rationale: Sambo's Mistakes, section II, urges Black people to unite around their race's vital interests; it speaks to unity more than to distinct political interests.

smash-state-machine.rationale: His provisional constitution expressly disclaims overthrowing state or federal governments and seeks amendment and repeal, though his armed actions challenged existing authority.

simple-living.rationale: His final family letter urges lasting contentment with moderate circumstances and limited worldly gains, taught by personal example.

no-denominational-politics.rationale: Sambo’s Mistakes, section III, criticizes abolitionists who refuse cooperation with allies because of differences between Christian denominations.

notes:
Declaration of Liberty (1859), Sambo's Mistakes and his prison letters could not be retrieved as full text, so they are not used; his final note is cited through Wikipedia. His trial speech denies any intent to incite insurrection, which conflicts with reports of his Harpers Ferry plan.

gpt-6.1-sol notes: Independent pass. The previous audit was read only for notes and sources. Downloaded Sanborn’s full 1885 Life and Letters and searched Brown’s own essays and letters by theme; used Sambo’s Mistakes (pp.128–131) and prison correspondence (chapter XIII) separately from the editor’s narrative. The Declaration of Liberty was retrieved but is not used to assign answers: its copyist/coauthor attribution requires care. The provisional constitution governs a proposed insurgent organization; its temporary communal stores are not treated as proof of a general socialist economic system. Every priority statement and all 490 statement texts were reviewed. Final review leaves all ten national-priority statements null: antislavery patriotism and retention of the American flag do not establish the broader nationalist propositions. Organising Black abolitionists is not a position on organising the working class by nation. The constitution’s prohibition of profanity is not evidence of punishing blasphemy or false religious worship. Neither religious belief nor recruitment by religious character establishes a preference for a single national church. Follow-up searches for the thin world, technology and ecology themes checked the collected letters for foreign affairs, nations, war, commerce, machinery, forests and animals. These mostly concerned his personal life, supporters’ views or the domestic antislavery campaign and did not establish further positions on those themes. Copy validation has no substantive errors and a legacy loosely-placed warning; the main lane should evaluate the merged record.
